Almost-complete builds and sets (using the same threshold above; minifigures have their own report on the Minifigures tab) where every missing part is fully covered by what's already sitting in a drawer or in a bag you’re partway through inventorying — gather these and they're done.

Builds where every part still missing is already sitting in a drawer — gather those and the build is done, whatever its size. Each build is checked against your drawers on its own, so where two of them need the same parts the list tells you which ones compete. A part counts as the same part when its part number and colour match, ignoring capital letters, spaces and hyphens ("Trans Red" and "Trans-Red" are treated alike).

    Select builds or sets

    Downloads an XML file in BrickLink's Wanted List format — on BrickLink, go to My Wanted Lists, open or create a list, click Upload, and choose this file. Part numbers are used as-is and assumed to match BrickLink's own catalog (usually true, but not always for older or variant parts). Colors are matched against a table of ~75 common BrickLink colors; anything not recognized is skipped and listed so you can add it by hand. Everything is marked "New" condition by default — change that on BrickLink afterward if you want used parts too.

    Checkmarks are saved as you go, so you can close this and pick up your shopping trip later.

    Upload parts for a build

    Works with a full CSV (Part Num, Quantity, Color, Description, elementId) or with Rebrickable's own parts-list export, which only includes Element ID and Quantity. Pick + New build in the dropdown to start a new build from the CSV (name it and, if you like, give it a theme). You can choose several CSV files at once (one per build) — each is matched to a build by its file name, or starts a new build, and you can change the match before importing — if Part Num is missing, each element ID is first looked up against parts already known elsewhere in the app (other builds, sets, or drawers), then against the Rebrickable API for anything still unmatched (uses the same API key entered on the Data & Tools tab). Anything that still can't be matched is imported with those fields left blank, so you can search for and fill them in afterward using "Incomplete info" on the MOC Parts tab. Leave Look up each part on Rebrickable ticked and every new line also gets its blank description and element ID filled in and a photo saved (to your site if GitHub Connection is set up) — values in your CSV are never overwritten, and the import is saved first, so a slow or failed lookup never loses rows.

    Track LEGO sets you own separately from your MOC builds. Get each set's part list from Rebrickable — either the reliable CSV download from their site, or a live API lookup if you have a free key.

    Fetch Parts and Names for New Sets

    Needs a free API key from rebrickable.com/api, set up on the Data & Tools tab. Browsers sometimes block this kind of cross-site request (the same issue we ran into with LEGO's own images) — if it fails for you, the CSV upload on the Import tab always works. Alongside the parts, this also looks up each set's official name and theme by its set number and updates them here — including overwriting anything you'd typed in manually. Spare parts Rebrickable lists with a set are ignored. Only fetches sets that don't already have parts on file, so it's fast to re-run after adding a new set — it won't re-download ones you already have. To refresh a set that already has parts (for example, to drop spares from an earlier import), open its Summary card and use Re-fetch parts from Rebrickable. Each new set's release year is filled in at the same time, and when GitHub Connection is set up its photo is saved to your site too. For sets you added before that, use Fix historic data below.

    These fill in or correct data for sets you added before a feature existed. New sets fetched above get all of this automatically.

    Fetch set photos and release years

    For sets added before these were automatic: looks each set up once on Rebrickable and fills in whatever it's missing — its release year, and its main photo (saved to your GitHub site's set-photos/ folder so it shows in the set's Summary on every device). A photo you uploaded yourself is never replaced. Needs your Rebrickable API key; photos also need GitHub Connection (Data & Tools tab) and are skipped without it. Safe to run again — sets that already have both are skipped.

    Fill in missing element IDs

    Scans every part line across MOC Builds, Official Sets, and Drawers for a part #/color combo with no element ID, and looks each one up on Rebrickable. Uses the Rebrickable API key set up on the Data & Tools tab. One lookup per unique part #/color combo — the result is applied to every matching line everywhere it appears, so a part missing its ID in five different builds only costs one request.

    Backfill missing photos

    Finds part lines with no photo — in your builds, your sets and your drawers — and fills them in from Rebrickable. It first checks every line (not just the ones you've already looked at), then looks each part up by part number and color, then by element ID, then by its BrickLink or LDraw number, and as a last resort a close variant of the part number (those are counted as “close matches”). Each photo is saved under the line's own element ID — uploaded to your site if GitHub Connection is set up (nothing is copied into the browser then, so it can't crowd out your data), otherwise saved in this browser. It paces its requests, retries when Rebrickable asks it to slow down, and when it finishes it tells you exactly why anything is still missing, with a CSV of those parts. Safe to run again: it skips anything that now has a photo.

    Re-fetch parts lists from Rebrickable

    Checks each set's parts list against Rebrickable's current one, the same as the Re-fetch parts button in a set's Summary, but for many sets at once. Check only looks — it lists which sets would change and how. Then Apply replaces the lists of the sets you leave ticked. Parts you'd marked short keep their shortfall; everything else counts as owned; spare parts are left out. Sets checked recently are skipped, so a repeat run only does the rest.

    Skip sets checked in the last

    Mark all sets complete

    Newly imported or fetched set parts are already assumed complete by default — this is only for fixing sets imported before that was the case, where some part lines still show as short even though you haven't actually used or lost anything from them. Sets every part line, across every official set you own, to fully on hand. This can't be undone, so only use it if your sets genuinely aren't missing anything right now — mark individual parts short afterward as needed.

    One repo, branch, and token used by everything below that talks to GitHub — publishing your collection, and (if you use it) the download script's auto-commit step. Saved in this browser so you don't have to retype it, but each browser needs it entered once.

    Copies Rebrickable’s photo of every part in your builds, official sets, minifigures and drawers into your site’s images/ folder, so your pictures don’t depend on Rebrickable. It runs in the background while the app is open, skips anything your site already has, and saves about one photo a second in batches (one commit per batch). New parts you add are picked up automatically. The first run on a big collection takes a while; it carries on where it left off each time you open the app.

    Use a fine-grained token (github.com → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens) scoped to only this one repository, with just "Contents: Read and write" permission — not a classic token with full account access. It's saved only in this browser and never sent anywhere except directly to GitHub; you can revoke it anytime from that same settings page.

    One API key used by everything that looks parts up on Rebrickable — the parts catalog search, autofill for descriptions and element IDs, fetching an official set's parts and name, and filling in missing element IDs. Needs a free key from rebrickable.com/api. Saved in this browser so you don't have to retype it, but each browser needs it entered once.

    Part/color lookups used by autofill and the parts catalog search are remembered on this device after the first time, so re-typing the same part later doesn't call Rebrickable again. This only lives in this browser — it isn't uploaded to your site. Clear it here if a part's catalog info looks out of date.

    Look up any part across your whole collection and refetch its details, element ID and photo from Rebrickable one part at a time — much quicker than a full refetch when only a few parts need it. Filters pick out parts with no photo, no description, no element ID, or not pulled recently.

    Your site’s data file lists every line in every build, set, minifigure and drawer. Right now each line also carries its own copy of its part’s description, element ID and photo address, even though the master list already holds them. For example, Plate 1×2 in Light Bluish Gray is written out 97 times. Turning this on writes those details once, in the master list, and leaves them off the lines. The app looks exactly the same, because it fills them back in when it loads.

    Before turning it on: versions of this page older than v2026.10.13.11 don’t know to fill the details back in. On every phone, tablet and computer you make changes from, open your site and refresh the page. Each one checks in below within a few seconds and shows Up to date. Devices that only view (no GitHub token) can’t save, so they don’t matter. If one you use isn’t listed, it hasn’t been opened with this version yet.

    Goes back over lists you've already imported — builds, official sets and drawers — and fills in what Rebrickable knows but your lines are missing: descriptions, element IDs, photos, and the part number and colour for lines that only have an element ID. It only fills blanks, so anything already on a line is left exactly as it was, and it saves as it goes. Use Check what's missing first to see how much there is. Needs the Rebrickable API key above; photos go to your site if GitHub Connection is set up, otherwise into this browser (stopping before it uses up the room your collection needs). Requests are paced, so a big collection takes a while — Stop any time and run it again later; it picks up where the blanks are.

    Skip lines already pulled from Rebrickable in the last

    Descriptions are replaced with Rebrickable's name for the part. An element ID is replaced only if it isn't one Rebrickable lists for that part and colour. Photos are downloaded again and overwrite the ones you have, including any you uploaded yourself. Part numbers and colours are never changed, only filled in when blank. It ignores the saved Rebrickable lookups so the data is fresh, which takes longer. Every line it pulls is tagged with the date, so the next refetch only touches lines that were never pulled or were pulled longer ago than the period above.

    Your site (data/inventory-data.json in your GitHub repo) is now the master copy. Every change you make here — MOC builds and parts, priority labels, shopping list checkmarks, official sets and their parts, drawers, and storage locations — auto-saves to your site a few seconds after you stop editing, and every time you open the app it loads the current version from your site first. Images aren't included in this sync — see Image Upload on the Images tab for those.

    Uses the GitHub Connection above. The buttons below are for manual use only — forcing an immediate save, or pulling the site's version again if you ever need to.

    Creates a timestamped snapshot of everything — builds, parts, sets, drawers, priorities, shopping checkmarks — saved as its own file in data/backups/ in your repo, separate from your live data. Uses the GitHub Connection above. Backups don't include images.

    Restore a backup

    Restoring replaces everything currently in this browser and on your site with an older snapshot — there's no undo beyond restoring yet another backup. To guard against doing this by accident, set a restore password below; you'll be asked for it every time, even on this device.

    Make, edit, copy, hide or delete the colour palettes the Recolour tool uses on a build or set.

    If the same physical piece is cataloged under two different part numbers (an old mold number, a duplicate listing, etc.), combine them here. Every row using the old number — across MOC builds, official sets, and drawers — is switched to the new number, and any lines that become duplicates of each other (same build/set/drawer and color) are merged into one, with quantities added together.

    Undo a merge

    Merged two parts that aren’t really the same? Enter them the same way round. Your site keeps every saved version of your data, so this finds the last one from before the merge and puts each line back as it was: lines that were the old part go back to it, and lines that were combined are split again. Changes you’ve made since are kept. Uses the GitHub Connection above.

    Compares this browser's data against what's currently published on your site, without changing anything. Use this before "Save to site" or "Load from site" if you're not sure which one has your latest work — especially useful when you use this on more than one device.

    Import a parts list CSV (e.g. exported from Google Sheets or Rebrickable) — or choose several files at once and they’re all imported together. New rows are added alongside your existing inventory — nothing gets overwritten. With the lookup box ticked, blank descriptions and element IDs are filled in from Rebrickable and photos are saved for the new rows.

    Recognized columns (any order, header names flexible): Part Num, Quantity, Color, Description, MOC Name, elementId, Amount on Hand, Built?, Priorty?. Only Part Num, Quantity, and MOC Name are required — the rest default to blank or zero.

    Already have a spreadsheet of everything you own (e.g. a Rebrickable or BrickLink export)? Upload it here to set the on-hand quantity for every matching part across all your builds in one go — this overwrites the on-hand numbers currently in the app for any part it matches.

    Needs a Part Num column and a Quantity column (however labeled — Qty, Owned, Amount, Stock, etc. are all recognized). A Color column is optional but recommended: if present, matching is by part number + color; if absent, matching is by part number alone across all colors of that part.

    On Rebrickable, open the set's page → "Parts" tab → download the CSV. No account or API key needed. Then pick which set it belongs to and upload it here. Minifigures work the same way: open the minifigure's page on Rebrickable, download its parts CSV, and pick the minifigure from the list. Spare parts (the extras Rebrickable lists separately from the set's real parts) are left out automatically. (You can also fetch a set's parts automatically via the Rebrickable API from the Official Sets tab.)

    Pick which drawer this CSV belongs to. Importing replaces that drawer's current contents — handy after a fresh recount. (For adding one part at a time instead, see the Drawers tab.)

    Recommended: host images with your site

    The most reliable option isn't caching in the browser at all — it's downloading the images once and putting them in your GitHub repo as real files, right next to index.html. Then they load instantly from your own site for every visitor, with no CORS proxy, no per-browser storage limit, and no dependence on lego.com staying reachable.

    1. Click "Generate download script" below — it builds a script listing every element ID currently in your inventory.
    2. Run python3 download_part_images.py on your own computer (needs internet; no extra installs required).
    3. It creates an images folder containing one .jpg per part, and can commit & push it for you automatically if run inside your repo folder.

    The app already checks images/<element id>.jpg on your site first, before ever trying a cache or lego.com — so this works automatically as soon as the folder exists. Whenever you add new parts, generate a fresh script and re-run it — it skips files it already has, so only the new element IDs get downloaded.

    Fallback: cache in this browser instead

    Once an image is cached here, it's stored in the app itself and will keep showing even with no internet connection.

    LEGO's own site blocks the direct download this feature needs (a browser security rule called CORS), so plain automatic caching usually fails silently. Turning this on routes image requests through images.weserv.nl, a free public image proxy, which re-serves the image with permission attached so caching can work. This means that third-party service sees which LEGO part images you're requesting. Off by default; the manual upload below never uses any third party.

    Needs internet the first time. Without the proxy above, most browsers will block this automatic download for cross-site images — if a part stays uncached after trying, use the manual upload below instead. Cached images are stored in this browser's local storage, which typically holds 5–10MB total — plenty for a few hundred thumbnails, but caching every part across all builds may eventually hit that limit.

    Or add images yourself: select image files whose filenames are the element ID (e.g. 6269079.jpg). No internet needed for this step.

    Parts Master List

    Your master list: one record for each part and colour, which every build, official set, minifigure and drawer takes its description, element ID and photo from. When any import or lookup finds better details for a part, they’re saved here and passed to every line that uses it. Each part shows the total you have across your whole collection. Press Where to see how many are in each drawer and each storage location. Refetch pulls just that part from Rebrickable again and updates every line that uses it — a few seconds each. Hover or long-press a description to see where the part is used.
